title: My Heart’s Wishes Rest with Asma, If Only They Were Within Reach
intro: Al-Buhturi praises al-Mutawakkil for making peace between factions of Taghlib. Al-Sayrafi places the poem around 243 AH (857–858 CE). From Asma’s alarm at the grey hair on a lover’s cheek, the journey leads to the caliph’s white palaces and a feud in which the men mourn the kinsmen they have killed. The measure of peace at the end is a mother who can breathe easily about her son.

translation: My heart’s wishes rest with Asma, if only they were within reach.
On that graceful girl it spends its longing and devotion.
1.sharh: Every wish his heart entertains takes the form of one woman. The small qualification about what is attainable cuts across an otherwise lavish declaration.

translation: Her turning away has frightened me. She turns
because the grey at my temple frightens her.
2.sharh: Her recoil and his alarm are expressed through forms of the same verb. Each is startled by what the other shows, a grey hair in one case and a withdrawal in the other.

translation: At the bend of the sand I took her love
upon a liver already weakened by its cracks.
3.sharh: Love comes with the weight of a load. In the physical imagination of this poetry the liver can bear grief, and his is already fissured by it.

translation: I used to follow beautiful women. Their follower
has always found fault with their fidelity.
4.sharh: The same word makes him first an individual follower and then one of a whole class. Complaints about fidelity seem to be an occupational hazard.

translation: Many a beauty has dealt unkindly with me.
Often I have loved a beauty whose conduct was ugly.
5.sharh: The Arabic for behaving well sounds like the word for beauty. He can tell good looks and good treatment apart, yet his affections keep choosing the first.

translation: I marvel that she shows dislike while I love her,
and that my heart defies me for love while I obey it.
6.sharh: His bewilderment moves inward. Asma will not return his affection, and his own heart refuses his authority, yet he faithfully serves them both.

translation: Sore-footed in the tangled darkness of night complain
camels of Ghurayr stock, their open range a waste.
7.sharh: The identity of the sufferers comes late in the sentence. Their breeding is distinguished, but pedigree offers their feet little protection on bare ground.

translation: I am a poor visitor of kings on sore-footed camels
unless their girths and straps hang loose.
8.sharh: The equipment was strapped tight when they set out. If it has begun to slip, the journey has worn enough flesh off the animals to prove the visitor’s determination.

translation: They make for the white palaces of Babylonia,
where al-Ghard and al-Badi' stand together.
9.sharh: Two named buildings give the journey a precise destination in Iraq. Their white surfaces stand out against the darkness the camels have crossed.

translation: Whenever the overlooking tower comes into view, they aim
at it the sunken eyes of mounts with threadbare cloths.
10.sharh: The word for casting a look usually suggests throwing something. The exhausted camels still have enough purpose to aim their eyes at the tower.

translation: Its gleam lights their course through the night
when a watch of darkness turns black around them.
11.sharh: The palace is already doing something for its visitors before they reach it. One flash of light gives them a bearing through a whole stretch of night.

translation: They go to see the Commander of the Faithful,
across the country’s broad and stretching plains.
12.sharh: Only now does he name the person at the end of the route. The broad spaces interposed in the second half recall what the camels have paid for the visit.

translation: Whenever we descend upon a town, its people repeat
tales of kindness that his generosity spreads.
13.sharh: The travellers hear about him afresh at every stop. His actual gifts have done the work a herald might otherwise have had to do.

translation: He guarded the bounds of Islam. Its enemies drew back,
knowing its stronghold could never be reached.
14.sharh: The proof of a strong defence is visible in the enemy’s decision. Knowing how well the territory is held, they keep away.

translation: When he tended his flock of subjects, the land’s
green and fertile pastures kept them from the barren ground.
15.sharh: The ruler appears as a herdsman with an eye for pasture. His flock can keep clear of a hungry tract because better grazing is available.

translation: I knew for certain, once Ja'far entrusted it
to God, that he would never let it go to ruin.
16.sharh: Ja'far’s act of trusting in God spells out his regnal name, al-Mutawakkil ala Allah. The title becomes a promise about the fate of the people in his care.

translation: He cleared doubt from our eyes with a caliphate
whose daybreak drove injustice and darkness from us.
17.sharh: The words for injustice and darkness are close in sound. One political sunrise can therefore drive away both the wrong and the obscurity that hid it.

translation: It is the sun. Its light discloses truth’s lustre,
and its rising shines into the secrets of hearts.
18.sharh: The sunrise now reaches two different interiors. It reveals truth to the eye and penetrates places in the heart where ordinary sunlight cannot go.

translation: I grieved for my mother’s people, Rabi'a,
when their strongholds decayed and their homes fell empty.
19.sharh: By calling Rabi'a his mother’s people he gives himself a family stake in the conflict. Its first casualties on view are inhabited places from which the inhabitants have vanished.

translation: Against my will their dwellings stood empty,
their haunts deserted and their company scattered.
20.sharh: The description moves from the houses, to the familiar places around them, to the company that gave those places life. Each is empty in a different way.

translation: They came to pass death round, who once were drinkers
taking their ease together and freely sharing wine.
21.sharh: Each side still hands something to the other. In the same gesture that once passed wine around a gathering, the kinsmen now dispense death.

translation: Whenever they part after one encounter, what brings them together
for the next is shed blood that cannot go unavenged.
22.sharh: The blood left by one battle acts almost like an appointment for the next. A family bound to answer a killing has no easy moment at which to stop.

translation: The gentle young woman reproaches her husband’s character
if he sleeps beside her with vengeance still unpaid.
23.sharh: The feud enters the marriage bed. Coming home safe can itself bring reproach if the husband has left a kinsman’s death unanswered.

translation: The heat of an ancient feud, a pride
like Kulayb’s, which no man could bend.
24.sharh: Kulayb’s name recalls the killing that set the old Basus war in motion. Pride that refuses to bow sounds different when the people paying for it belong to the same family.

translation: And riders of battle, whose breasts seethe
with grudges till their coats of mail grow tight.
25.sharh: Mail normally gives the fighter room to breathe and move. Here hatred has swollen inside him until even the iron seems to close in.

translation: In vengeance they kill the lives they hold most dear,
with hands that scarcely will obey them.
26.sharh: The victim is indispensable to the avenger as kin. The hand’s hesitation lets a reader see the love that the public duty of vengeance suppresses.

translation: When they fight and their blood pours out,
they remember kinship, and their tears pour out.
27.sharh: A single Arabic verb serves for both flows. The men shedding tears over a kinsman are the very men who have shed his blood.

translation: Interlocking spears cut apart between them
interlocking ties of kin, whose cutter earns blame.
28.sharh: One adjective describes spear shafts crossing and family ties branching into one another. Cutting the second tangle is an offence even when the first makes it possible.

translation: Without the Commander of the Faithful and his bounty,
shirt fronts would once more wear blood for perfume.
29.sharh: The marks a perfume leaves at the opening of a garment give the bloodstains their name. What looks from a distance like adornment would be the trace of another killing.

translation: The very root of Taghlib would have been cut out,
the root that kept its branches and shoots alive.
30.sharh: The factions are branches of a single stock. Destroying the root in the course of their fight would put an end even to the branch that seemed to win.

translation: You lifted Taghlib daughter of Wa'il by both arms
when she had lost hope that her fallen one might rise.
31.sharh: An ancestor’s name ordinarily suggests a man. Here the tribe itself appears as Wa'il’s daughter, lifted bodily by both arms from what seemed a fatal fall.

translation: You, God’s trustee, were guardian of her life.
Your own retainer Fath pleaded for her that day.
32.sharh: Two different relationships meet in the word for patron or client. Taghlib owes its life to the caliph, and Fath uses his own closeness to that ruler to speak for the tribe.

translation: By my life, you honoured him with a kindness
towards them, a favour he spread throughout their people.
33.sharh: The benefit goes to the tribe and the honour of distributing it to Fath. The pronouns keep the ruler, his envoy and the recipients distinct.

translation: He drew them together after jealous points of honour
had driven them apart and were slow to relent.
34.sharh: Fath had to win over people whose sense of what honour demanded had helped scatter them. Such loyalties take longer to change than a formal decision.

translation: Their wanderer saw the open road and found his way.
Their extremist drew back, their distance narrowed.
35.sharh: The reconciliation has a geography of its own. The lost can see a road, the man who has gone too far can stop, and those once far apart come nearer.

translation: He passed judgement among them. They drew apart,
the lowly and the high alike content with it.
36.sharh: To draw apart here is to stop grappling. The settlement’s authority shows in the assent it wins at both ends of the social scale.

translation: The brown lances now stand planted, and the slender blades
are sheathed, the rough and the polished alike.
37.sharh: The spears are planted and the swords put away. The distinction between a roughly finished blade and a polished one has ceased to matter in peacetime.

translation: Hearts once loud with pounding are still.
Eyes that scarcely slept have gone to sleep.
38.sharh: The paired changes can be felt without seeing a battlefield. A quiet pulse and an undisturbed night tell the inhabitants what peace means.

translation: They come to you with their good sense restored,
their desisting has put what you hated far from them.
39.sharh: The delegation’s change of conduct precedes its words of thanks. To have recovered their judgement is to have put some distance between themselves and the feud.

translation: They return again and again to praise like
strips of upland meadow lavishly watered in spring.
40.sharh: Their praise does not go stale in repetition. He sees its successive passages as long bright strips of an upland meadow after good rain.

translation: They turn away, ashamed that you should see those faces.
The rebels sinned, and the obedient were blamed.
41.sharh: Even the members who had obeyed feel the shame of appearing before the caliph. A collective name has made the innocent answer for someone else’s act.

translation: Their only excuse is that even the wise man’s forbearance
was swept into folly by his tribe’s outlaw.
42.sharh: A tribe’s reckless member can set events in motion that unseat even a prudent man’s judgement. Forbearance itself is said to behave foolishly.

translation: Many a mother feared death for her son
at the first clash of massed fighters.
43.sharh: He moves away from the public audience to one woman. Her fear begins before the battle, at the thought of the first meeting of armies.

translation: By making peace you steadied her startled heart.
Her inward fear subsided, her ribs grew still.
44.sharh: The previous bayt’s unnamed mother receives the direct benefit. Her heart was like something tethered that had broken loose. In the quiet of her chest, he locates the caliph’s achievement.

translation: Live long. How many of Taghlib you have kept alive
by pardon, till even the lame could walk strongly again.
45.sharh: The wish for the caliph to survive echoes his saving of the tribe. She was lifted from the ground earlier, and by the final word she is walking under her own power.

1.1.4.head: أَسماء
1.1.4.meaning: Asma, the woman addressed in the opening love verses.

2.2.4.head: عِذار
2.2.4.meaning: The hair along the side of the face.

3.1.4-5.head: مُنعَرَج اللِّوى
3.1.4-5.meaning: “The bend of the sand”, the curve of a sandy ridge remembered as a meeting place.

7.1.2.meaning: Tenderness in a camel’s foot from going bare over rough ground.

7.2.1.head: غُرَيرِيَّة
7.2.1.meaning: Ghurayri, descended from the camel sire al-Ghurayr.

7.2.3.head: مَرت
7.2.3.meaning: A barren, treeless stretch of country.

7.2.4.head: بَقيع
7.2.4.meaning: An expanse of ground, here stripped of pasture.

8.2.5.head: نُسوع
8.2.5.meaning: Broad leather straps for saddles and loads.

9.1.6.head: بابِل
9.1.6.meaning: Babil, Babylonia, the Iraqi region towards which he rides.

9.2.3.head: غَرد
9.2.3.meaning: Al-Ghard, a palace of al-Mutawakkil near the Tigris. Its name has several transmitted forms.

9.2.4.head: البَديع
9.2.4.meaning: Al-Badi', a palace at Samarra, al-Mutawakkil’s seat.

10.2.2.head: خوص
10.2.2.meaning: Camels with deep-set or sunken eyes.

10.2.5.head: قُطوع
10.2.5.meaning: Cloths spread on the camels beneath their saddles.

11.2.6.head: هَزيع
11.2.6.meaning: A watch or portion of the night.

14.1.2.head: حَوزَة
14.1.2.meaning: A community’s territory and the bounds it defends.

15.1.3.head: سِرب
15.1.3.meaning: A flock or herd, here the people in the caliph’s care.

16.1.5.head: جَعفَر
16.1.5.meaning: Ja'far ibn al-Mu'tasim, the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil.

17.2.5.head: صَديع
17.2.5.meaning: Daybreak, imagined as splitting the darkness.

19.1.3.head: رَبيعَة
19.1.3.meaning: Rabi'a, the larger tribal group to which Taghlib belonged.

19.2.1.head: مَصانِع
19.2.1.meaning: Built settlements, strongholds or substantial buildings.

20.2.2.head: مَغانٍ
20.2.2.meaning: Former dwelling places and familiar haunts.

21.2.4.head: رِفه
21.2.4.meaning: In ease, with a plentiful supply.

22.2.4.head: أُطِلَّ
22.2.4.meaning: Is allowed to go unavenged, of shed blood.

22.2.5.head: نَجيع
22.2.5.meaning: Dark blood shed from a wound.

24.2.1.head: كُلَيبِيَّة
24.2.1.meaning: Kulaybi, recalling the pride of Kulayb, whose killing set off the Basus war.

26.1.3.head: وِتر
26.1.3.meaning: A blood debt from an earlier killing.

28.1.1.head: شَواجِر
28.1.1.meaning: Interlaced or crossing, of spear shafts.

28.2.4.head: قَطوع
28.2.4.meaning: A person who repeatedly severs kinship ties.

29.1.4.head: طَول
29.1.4.meaning: Bounty and ability to confer favours.

29.2.4.head: رُدوع
29.2.4.meaning: Stains left by a coloured perfume, here bloodstains.

30.1.1.head: اُصطُلِمَ
30.1.1.meaning: Was cut off at the root.

30.1.2.head: جُرثومَة
30.1.2.meaning: The root stock from which a family or a tree grows.

31.1.2.head: ضَبع
31.1.2.meaning: The upper arms, by which a fallen person can be lifted.

31.1.3-5.head: تَغلِب اِبنَة وائِل
31.1.3-5.meaning: Taghlib, a tribe descended from Wa'il, personified here as his daughter.

32.2.2.head: فَتح
32.2.2.meaning: Fath ibn Khaqan, a close associate of al-Mutawakkil and mediator in the settlement.

34.2.1.head: حَفائِظ
34.2.1.meaning: Points of honour that move a person to defend what he holds dear.

37.2.3.head: مَجفُوّ
37.2.3.meaning: A rough or coarsely finished blade.

37.2.4.head: صَنيع
37.2.4.meaning: A blade carefully finished and maintained.

39.2.4.head: نُزوع
39.2.4.meaning: Desisting from a course of action.

40.2.1.head: سَبائِب
40.2.1.meaning: Long strips, like lengths cut from a cloth.

40.2.2-3.head: رَوض الحَزن
40.2.2-3.meaning: “Upland meadows”, pasture watered on higher, rougher ground.

42.2.5.head: خَليع
42.2.5.meaning: A reckless member who has cast off his tribe’s restraints.

44.1.4-5.head: نافِر جَأشِها
44.1.4-5.meaning: “Her bolting spirit”, her heart in a state of alarm.

45.2.5.head: ظَليع
45.2.5.meaning: Someone who limps. The war has left Taghlib limping, and peace restores its footing. The opening consonant can sound like ض in the recitation. Both editions give ظ.
